story_text.value:
ThinkRail is JetBrains' open-source IDE shell for AI coding agents: worktree-per-tab, chat + file tree + terminal, but hardwired to one agent (Pi).

My fork adds a plugin API so it can host others too, starting with Claude Code running in the same UI.

What's new over upstream:

- A prototype of real plugin system - Claude Code as a first-class citizen — config, IDE bridge, and terminal status all wired in as a builtin plugin, so you get Claude Code sessions in the same worktree-scoped UI as `pi`. - Seven other builtin plugins split out the same way: blueprint (interactive specs), PDF preview, branch graph, a live drawing/visualize surface, and file-type icons

Nightly builds via a Homebrew tap are provided.

title.value: Show HN: I forked JetBrains' new agent IDE to host Claude Code

story_text.value:
I spent a while exploring whether AI could help build businesses that operate with little ongoing owner involvement. This was inspired in part by Andon Labs’ Vending-Bench work on AI agents running simulated businesses. Their Project Vend collaboration with Anthropic takes that question into a real shop. (Obviously it was also inspired by "the dream.")

Unfortunately, currently, I think the answer is generally "no." Vending-Bench shows outcomes relative to a well-defined business environment, while starting businesses isn't well-defined and much harder, for us and AI.

But one useful result was this browser simulation, which I'm sharing as a free side project. It basically generalizes the idea behind Vending-Bench itself, but in a simulation that anyone can mess around with, including AI.

Choose a digital product, custom digital service, vending machine, or reusable equipment such as a laundromat. Set demand, costs, staffing and rules, then run 14 simulated days without the owner. Inspect unfinished orders, cash, refunds and requests for your help. Change the setup and rerun the same conditions.

The model supplies fictional customers and failures. AI help has preset outcomes; no model is called by the site. It's a way to explore operating assumptions, not a demand or profit forecast. An optional copy/paste workflow lets your own assistant plan decisions with the fictional fortnight known in advance. It is not thinking live between days.

I developed it with substantial AI coding assistance, automated checks, AI role-playing of users (occupying user types/roles), and feedback from human friends who tried it. It runs in the browser without signup.

Repo here: https://github.com/automatedteach/vending-machine-lab

title.value: Show HN: Vending Machine Lab – Build business, leave for 2 wks, see what breaks

story_text.value:
I'm the builder of LEO, and this is not a packege or a service.

It's a engineering framework of the rules for Cursor or ClaudeCode, helping to build enorm AI Native projects, 300 000 + lines of code (I understand that is not the quality gate, but - zero TODO, cyclomatic complexity <= 10 (lizard), the project work). A cursorrules file with 44 rules plus 133 *.md files (roles, canons, protocols) that registred how to do an Enterprise project. However, I build solo an AI Nodes Constructor pipeline IDE like n8n for 3-4 month, and if you wont you can look some greps and tests of this project.

368 schema constrants, 77 row-level-security policies, 120+ alembic migrations, 3900+ tests, 10 200+ functions and more.

If you wont to know more about the project and LEO rules: https://dev.to/alex-zaporozhan/385000-lines-of-code-in-three...

Another projects build with LEO (first debute project, open source, enjoy the lines of code): https://github.com/alex-zaporozhan/medCore"

Thank you for your help,

Alex

story_text.value:
Like a lot of folks, I'm trying to understand the AI reality vs. the hype cycle. I have my own experiences both using it and seeing it rolled out with a “do more AI” mandate at a huge tech company. Even looking here at discussions we have the full spectrum from engineers who say they don’t code anymore, they just manage agents, to engineers who say they find it basically useless because of how stupid it is. I’ve been looking for clues (I wanted to use the word “signals" there but I can’t because I don’t want you all to think Claude wrote this) in the market that we can all see, so we don’t have to accept “trust me bro, AI solved coding”.

Here’s my question:

Where is all of the AI coded software?

If coding is a nearly solved problem, if AI is making it so easy to make anything, why aren't we seeing the market flood with cheap alternatives to software that we all use daily and hate?

Microsoft office, anything from Adobe, Jira

Make your own list. Every designer I’ve ever met hates Adobe and their subscription model. My company spends a hojillion dollars a year on office365 and everyone hates it. Why aren’t we seeing alternatives popping up?

Should we be expecting this as a part of the whole “democratization” promise of AI?

As an addendum: I picked office and adobe just because they are two things we always whine about in tech, I realize they are platforms/ecosystems now, maybe it would be better to say Word and Photoshop, etc. but substitute in any commercial software you want. If AI coding can take over the internet application space can’t it also take over the software application space?

title.value: Ask HN: Where is all of the AI coded software?
